strengths: Technically sound three-stage training framework combining UVMC learning, UVMC-guided pretraining, and task-specific fine-tuning with clear mathematical formulations (Eqs. 1-8, 9)
Comprehensive experimental validation with 14,000+ rollouts across 6 heterogeneous robot embodiments and 120+ manipulation tasks, substantially exceeding typical robotics papers
Well-designed ablation studies (Tables 4-5) systematically isolating contributions of dataset pretraining, UVMC learning, and cross-modal alignment, showing each component matters
Demonstrated generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios including unseen objects, illumination changes, and background variations (Figure 7, Table 3), suggesting learning of robust features
Strong and consistent improvements over multiple state-of-the-art baselines (π₀, π₀, RDT, UniVLA, GR0OT-N1.5) across diverse robot configurations and task types
Fast adaptation capability to novel tasks with limited demonstrations (20-shot, Figure 6), showing practical applicability
Detailed implementation documentation including hyperparameters (Tables 6-8), architecture specifications (Appendix 6.2), and dataset curation procedures (Appendix 6.3) support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the work is primarily engineering of existing techniques (dual-branch VQ-VAE, cross-modal alignment via KL divergence, standard VLA backbone). UVMC builds on prior action tokenization work (Shafullah et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2025b) without substantial conceptual breakthrough

Insufficient theoretical justification for core claim: why discrete vision-motion codes specifically improve generalization is not rigorously established. The paper lacks analysis of what patterns UVMC captures or why this intermediate representation outperforms alternatives

No comparison to end-to-end learning without UVMC intermediate stage on identical data; necessity of the proposed representation unclear when other methods might achieve similar results with simpler architectures

Ad-hoc design choices with insufficient justification: nearest-neighbor quantization (Eqs. 5-6) vs. alternatives unexplored, β parameter (0.25) lacks sensitivity analysis, alignment regularization weight requires careful tuning but guidance minimal

Modest empirical improvements: many results show 5-15% gains over baselines despite the added complexity; practical significance of improvements questionable given the substantial increase in training procedures

High computational costs (38,400 GPU hours) and scalability limitations not adequately addressed; all evaluation on manipulation tasks only—applicability to navigation, grasp-only, or other robot capabilities unexplored

Missing failure analysis and interpretability: success rates plateau at 30-40% on harder tasks but root causes unexplored; no interpretation of what visual/motion patterns UVMC codes learn or when the approach fails

No statistical significance testing: error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests across multiple runs absent; reproducibility limited by undisclosed code availability and underspecified data sampling strategy

Incomplete technical details: gradient flow through quantization operations needs clearer treatment; dataset sampling procedure and validation set selection procedure underspecified; limited inference latency analysis despite mentioning 200 Hz operation

Limited evaluation metrics: only success rates reported; missing trajectory quality metrics, force profile analysis, error distributions, or robustness analysis to sensor noise—important for real-world deployment

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation across 6 heterogeneous robot embodiments with 14,000+ rollouts demonstrates significant experimental breadth and rigor
Comprehensive three-stage training pipeline (UVMC learning → pretraining → finetuning) is well-motivated and systematically executed
Consistent improvements over multiple strong baselines (π₀, R₀, RDT, UnVLA, GROOT-N1.5) across diverse tasks and platforms
Thoughtful ablation studies (Section 4.4) examining lightweight models, UVMC components, and cross-modal alignment contributions
Detailed task specifications and hyperparameters in appendices support reproducibility efforts
Honest reporting of out-of-box generalization gaps (Figure 5, Table 3) and limitations of the approach
weaknesses: UVMC represents an incremental technical contribution—essentially a standard VQ-VAE with a cross-modality KL-divergence alignment term. The paper lacks theoretical justification for why this specific unified factorization is superior to alternatives (e.g., separate vision/motion codes with explicit alignment)

Unfair experimental comparisons: XR-1 receives Stage-1 (0.9B UVMC pretraining) + Stage-2 (large-scale pretraining on diverse data) + Stage-3 (task-specific finetuning), while baselines are often trained from scratch or with minimal pretraining, inflating apparent advantages

Severe generalization limitations undermine claims of versatility: out-of-box evaluation shows significant performance drops (Figure 5 drops from ~70% to 30-50%), revealing heavy dependence on task-specific supervision rather than genuine cross-task generalization

Limited novelty in the overall paradigm—the three-stage (pretrain → pretrain → finetune) approach mirrors existing VLM-robotics work (RT-1, RT-2, Open-X). The distinguishing contribution (UVMC) is insufficient to warrant acceptance at a top venue
Modest empirical improvements: many task comparisons show only 5-15% gains (e.g., Table 14 shows 72.3% vs 67% for π₀). Improvements are statistically significant but not transformative
Computational barriers to reproducibility: 38,400 GPU hours required for full training; code availability not mentioned; high computational cost limits accessibility and verification by the community

Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance metrics despite claiming 14,000 rollouts. Unclear if these represent independent trials or weighted replicates across tasks

Insufficient technical justification: no ablation comparing unified codes vs. separate codes with alignment; no analysis of quantization bottleneck (Eqs. 5-6) impact; no investigation of dataset imbalance effects (Table 9 shows 40-45% from Open-X/Language Table vs 10% from EgoD4)

Dense presentation of methodology (Section 3.2-3.4): heavy mathematical notation introduced without clear intuitive motivation; readers must decipher why specific loss combinations and architectural choices were selected

Generalization analysis reveals fundamental limitation: Tasks unseen during pretraining (Stage 1-2) require Stage-3 fine-tuning, indicating the learned representations do not achieve meaningful cross-task transfer

strengths: Technically sound methodology with well-motivated design: UVMC architecture clearly addresses limitations of existing VLA models by jointly encoding visual dynamics and action motion, with principled cross-modality alignment via KL-divergence loss

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across 6 distinct robot platforms spanning 120+ diverse manipulation tasks with 14,000 rollouts; consistent 10-30% improvements over strong baselines (π0, RDT, UniVLA, GR00T-N1.5)

Strong generalization capabilities: Out-of-box evaluation shows only 0.9% performance degradation despite task diversity; robust to novel objects, backgrounds, illumination changes, and dynamic distractors; fast adaptation with limited demonstrations (20-shot) outperforms single-task baselines

Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear logical flow from motivation to methodology to results; detailed appendices with hyperparameters (Tables 6-8), all 120+ task specifications (Tables 15-21), dataset statistics (Table 9); systematic ablations (Tables 4-5) clearly demonstrate each component's contribution

Practical contributions and design flexibility: Three-stage training pipeline enables effective knowledge capture while maintaining computational efficiency; lightweight variant (XR-1-Light) shows applicability to resource-constrained settings; clear task-specific post-training strategy

Principled cross-embodiment knowledge transfer: Table 5 demonstrates that UVMC learning provides 15% absolute improvement in cross-embodiment transfer, with additional benefits from cross-modal alignment (20% gain) and dataset scaling (65%→100% with full Stage-1 data)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (VQ-VAE from 2017, cross-modal alignment losses, multi-stage training) are individually well-established; the contribution is primarily their engineering-focused combination rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Insufficient theoretical analysis: No principled explanation for why discrete quantization specifically enables multimodal alignment; missing comparisons with continuous latent representations (standard VAE) or alternative quantization schemes; codebook learning dynamics not explored

Underexplored representation learning: No visualization or clustering analysis of learned 512-dimensional codes; unclear what visual dynamics codes represent versus action codes; no evidence codes are semantically meaningful across embodiments; transfer mechanism explanation is superficial

Prohibitive computational requirements: Stage 1 pretraining requires 38,400 GPU hours on 80 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, creating significant barriers to reproducibility and accessibility; limited discussion of computational efficiency or potential optimizations for resource-constrained settings

Narrow evaluation scope and limited generalization analysis: All evaluated tasks are manipulation-only; generalization to navigation, mobile manipulation, or other embodied AI domains unclear; Table 3 generalization results limited to two scenario types (DFR-SweepTrash and DFR-HangCup) without systematic failure case analysis

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons with other discrete representation methods (VQ-GAN, alternative quantization schemes) and continuous latent baselines; only compares against four recent VLA approaches; limited comparison of design choices (e.g., codebook size selection)

strengths: Impressive empirical scale with 14,000+ rollouts across 6 embodiments and 120+ manipulation tasks, demonstrating comprehensive evaluation
Novel UVMC concept elegantly addresses cross-embodiment VLA by jointly encoding visual dynamics and motor control through dual-branch VQ-VAE
Consistent and substantial improvements over strong baselines (10-25% gains across diverse embodiments and tasks)
Thorough experimental validation including ablations, unseen scenario evaluation, cross-embodiment transfer analysis, fast adaptation experiments, and simulation results on CALVIN
Excellent reproducibility support with detailed architecture specifications, hyperparameter tables, comprehensive dataset statistics, and complete task descriptions with visualizations
Insightful representation analysis demonstrating UVMC learns semantically meaningful, embodiment-agnostic representations (Figures 12-15)
Practical framework variants (XR-1-Light with 230M parameters) addressing deployment constraints
Well-organized presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited fundamental technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (VQ-VAE, dual-branch encoders) in robotics context rather than introducing novel methods
Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why UVMC works: lacks justification for superiority of discrete quantization over continuous representations, limited quantization analysis
Significant dataset composition bias with OXE comprising 77.3% of pretraining episodes, no systematic analysis of representation sensitivity to dataset weighting
Experimental design concerns: different baselines use different datasets/backbones limiting fair comparison, limited hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, no isolation of Stage-3 contribution
Generalization claims require caveats: out-of-box evaluation has 0.45% data overlap, most tasks <85% success, fast adaptation uses relatively high supervision (20 demos per task)
Massive computational cost (77,400+ GPU hours) substantially limits reproducibility and broader adoption, no computational efficiency comparison with baselines
Limited cross-embodiment transfer analysis: Table 16 shows only 2 tasks, missing systematic analysis of which task properties enable/prevent transfer
Quantitative representation analysis gaps: uses only qualitative t-SNE visualizations, lacks metrics for disentanglement, mutual information, or embodiment-agnosticity
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; variance handling unclear
Missing comparisons with recent vision-language foundation models and alternative discrete representation schemes
Task independence concerns: Figure 14 shows substantial semantic clustering among 120 tasks, unclear whether improvements stem from task diversity or method
Practical deployment underexplored: limited discussion of latency, real-time constraints, failure modes, or safety considerations in practice

strengths: Large-scale empirical validation: 14,000+ rollouts across 6 diverse robot embodiments with 120+ manipulation tasks demonstrates substantial engineering effort and comprehensive evaluation scope
Consistent empirical improvements: XR-1 outperforms strong baselines (π₀, RDT, GROOT-N1.5, UniVLA) across all six robots with average gains of 5-30% across task distributions
Comprehensive experimental analysis: Extensive ablations (Tables 3, 14-16), generalization studies (Table 4), and qualitative visualizations (Figures 12-15) provide good empirical characterization
Large-scale curated dataset: XR-D with 158K episodes covering 6 embodiments could serve as valuable resource for future robotics research
Implementation transparency: Detailed hyperparameters (Tables 5-7), training procedures, and architectural choices enable reasonable reproducibility
Cross-embodiment transfer: Demonstrates that pretraining on diverse data can improve performance on multiple platforms, with some zero-shot capabilities
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with effective visualizations and comprehensive appendices documenting all 120 tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution (UVMC) is a straightforward application of VQ-VAE to encode joint vision-motion codes; no fundamental methodological innovation beyond combining existing techniques at scale

Unjustified design choices: Why unified vision-motion codes are superior to separate representations lacks theoretical justification; critical design decisions (β=0.25, codebook dimensionality, alignment loss design) appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

Unclear UVMC mechanism: The paper asserts but doesn't convincingly demonstrate how discrete codes bridge embodiment gaps with different action spaces or how the alignment loss (Eq. 3) achieves embodiment-agnostic consistency
Incomplete ablations: Ablations don't cleanly isolate whether improvements come from UVMC specifically versus large-scale pretraining and dataset diversity alone

Overstated generalization claims: Despite 'general-purpose' framing, method requires extensive per-embodiment fine-tuning (Table 3 shows Stage-3 is critical); no true zero-shot transfer to novel embodiments demonstrated
Incremental performance gains: Improvements are typically 5-20% over baselines; many tasks still show <50% success rates (Tables 9-13), limiting practical deployment value
High computational overhead: Three-stage training requires 38,400 GPU-hours for pretraining, making reproduction infeasible for most researchers and real-world adoption unlikely
Baseline fairness concerns: Some baselines achieve surprisingly low performance (<30% on multiple tasks), raising questions about implementation quality and whether comparisons are fair

Insufficient analysis depth: Paper lacks mechanistic insights into why UVMC works; visualizations are helpful but don't provide fundamental understanding; failure mode analysis (Section H) is qualitative only
XR-1-Light underdeveloped: Lightweight variant (230M params) is barely analyzed despite being potentially more practical; architecture choices appear unmotivated
Task-specific fine-tuning essential: Effectiveness heavily dependent on per-task fine-tuning, contradicting 'versatile foundation model' positioning

Limited novelty of components: VQ-VAE motion encoding is established (BehaviorTransformers, MotionTokenizer); vision-language-action pipeline is standard (π₀, RT-X); cross-modality alignment via KL divergence is vanilla
Dataset bias not addressed: Pretraining data heavily skewed (OXE 40%, XR-D 35%, RoboMIND 15%); unclear how weighting affects embodiment-specific performance
Weak generalization evidence: Out-of-distribution evaluation uses only 0.45% of XR-D; truly novel embodiments/tasks outside pretraining distribution not tested

strengths: Exceptional scale of real-world empirical validation: 14,000+ rollouts across 6 distinct robot embodiments with 120+ diverse manipulation tasks demonstrates rare breadth in robotics research
Consistent and substantial improvements over strong baselines across all evaluated embodiments (e.g., 73.5% vs 37.3% on Dual-Arm UR-Se)

Comprehensive experimental analysis including thorough ablations (Tables 3, 14-16), out-of-distribution evaluation, fast adaptation studies, and detailed failure case analysis with clear categorization
Well-designed three-stage training paradigm that is logical and well-motivated, with UVMC serving as an effective intermediate representation for cross-modal knowledge transfer
Excellent reproducibility documentation with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, dataset composition tables, and complete task specifications with instructions for all 120 tasks
Insightful representational analysis showing semantic organization of UVMC space through t-SNE visualization and nearest-neighbor retrieval demonstrating embodiment-agnostic action understanding
Practical system efficiency enabling deployment without massive computational resources (5Hz inference on standard hardware)
Strong cross-embodiment knowledge transfer capability demonstrated through Table 16, showing that shared visual-motion representations improve performance on diverse platforms
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: UVMC is a straightforward dual-branch VQ-VAE application; three-stage training is well-established; contribution is primarily system-level engineering rather than algorithmic innovation

Insufficient theoretical justification for design choices: no clear explanation for why joint visual-motion encoding is optimal; modest ablation improvements (~5%) in Table 14 raise questions about UVMC necessity; no analysis of what enables generalization

Lack of statistical rigor despite large-scale evaluation: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; claims of 'significantly higher' performance are not formally supported; no inter-rater agreement metrics for human evaluation

Limited and somewhat dated baseline comparisons: missing recent strong VLA methods; extreme baseline failures on unseen embodiments (π₀: 0% on Tien Kung 2.0) raise fairness concerns; no convergence or sample efficiency analysis

Reproducibility barriers despite good documentation: requires 38,400 GPU hours per stage beyond reach of most labs; key datasets (RoboMIND, XR-D) not publicly available; no code availability mentioned
Incomplete failure analysis: failure categorization is primarily qualitative; no systematic breakdown across task types; limited exploration of precision deficiency root causes in multi-arm scenarios

Missing analyses on important dimensions: no sample efficiency comparison, data necessity analysis, or convergence curves; no investigation of why three-stage approach is beneficial; task difficulty not quantified

Evaluation methodology concerns: human evaluation metric lacks documentation of rater selection and agreement; 120 tasks share similar pick-place structure despite diversity claims; success metrics could be more objective

Scope limitations of 'versatile' claims: all evaluation on manipulation robots only; no navigation, locomotion or other modalities; 'embodiment-agnostic' claim overstated given embodiment-specific training requirements
